en: Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
An Elucidation of the Four Protections:
Contemplation of the Body.
1. Discourse on Immorality, 2.
Discourse on the Benefits of Virtue, 3.
Discourse on Exhortation.
4. Discourse on the Conduct of Resident Monks;
5. Discourse on the Relinquishing of Requisites;
6. Discourse on the Pāṭimokkha.
7. The Discourse on Advice to the Donor:
The Promise of Homage.
The world-systems by the tens of millions, kissed by the multitude of gods;
May the lotus-foot of the Buddha rest upon my head, born from the fragrance of his compassion.
I pay homage to the Victor, who has emerged from the infinite world-systems and is filled with a multitude of virtues;
and to the Dhamma worshipped by him, and to the stainless Saṅgha belonging to it.
I shall now explain the four protections, which are the very words of the Fully Enlightened One;
this brings about heedfulness and should be heard by those who fear existence. These are:
recollection of the Buddha, mindfulness of death, loving-kindness toward all beings, and the cultivation of equanimity.
Guarding through diligence is the fourfold honor of the virtuous:
1. The cultivation of mindfulness of the Buddha; 2.
The cultivation of mindfulness of death.
3. Meditation on the foul (aśubha-bhāvanā), 4.
Meditation on loving-kindness (maitrī-bhāvanā);
remembering the Buddha’s exhortation, those who fear death and seek happiness [should practice these].
Those who abide in the water of the Subhameṭṭha attain even greater coolness than Sītā herself.
This word of the Fully Enlightened One is like water for warding off the fire of death;
many who were scorched by that fire found coolness through this water.
Having fortified one's faith through recollection of the Buddha, one should subdue conceit by reflecting on death;
the wise person should destroy lust with the meditation on foulness, and hatred with loving-kindness.
1. Exposition of the Recollection of the Buddha.
The Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the bestower of knowledge, vision, and conduct;
the Well-Gone One, the one who has gone to the good destination, the Teacher, the All-Knowing Blessed One, the Unconquered.
Because he is far removed and because he has slain the evil doer, he is called "Arahant."
Having destroyed the wheel of rebirth, he is worthy of worship; being worthy of honor, let us bow to the Arahat.
Having thoroughly inspired the householders, the Victor delivered a graduated discourse;
revealing the Truths by day, he bestowed supreme satisfaction.
In the first watch of the night, he gave the nectar-medicine to the bhikkhus;
for the gods born in the field of birth, he was the cutter of doubt in the middle watch;
at the beginning, he experienced the bliss of the fruit, and in the middle, the Victor attained the supreme state.
The world’s disciples were to be reached at the end of the aeon, even when divided into three parts.
Disregarding weariness, the Protector bore the burden of five Buddhas’ work;
like one who has mastered the Teacher’s art, he was intent on the welfare of others, possessed of great compassion.
The Buddha instructed the monks: "Having walked back and forth and having sat down, one should meditate by day and night; one may sleep only during the middle watch.
There is no time for sleeping in the teaching of that Great Hero."
Out of heedlessness toward the Lord of Sages, one who is grateful and esteemed as virtuous should not fail to strive—
having gone into solitude and being diligent— for the sake of knowing what is unknown and for attaining what has not been attained.
Exert yourselves, strive, apply yourselves to the Buddha’s teaching;
shake off the army of Death as an elephant shakes down a reed-hut.
Whoever shall dwell heedfully in this Dhamma and Discipline—
"Having abandoned the cycle of birth, he will make an end of suffering"—
this was our exhortation, a remembrance of the liberation of the Liberated One;
it was not at all for the sake of negligence toward the Greatly Compassionate Teacher.
Through doubting the Sutta, by doing what should not be done,
or by wasting time in vain, the dull-witted person brings about the end of suffering— how could such a one do so?
The sky, the world-system, sentient beings, and even the qualities of a Buddha— [all these are inconceivable].
There are four named "Infinite," for which no limit exists.
Just as one cannot measure the sky or space with fingers, cords,
or measuring rods, so too can no one measure its virtue.
2. Exposition of Mindfulness of Death:
One who desires mindfulness of death should first listen to the word of the Buddha with an undistracted mind; this is the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
The life of mortals here is signless and unknown,
meager, limited, and joined with suffering.
There is indeed no such effort by which those who are born could escape.
Having reached old age, one reaches death; for such is the nature of living beings.
Just as ripe fruits have the fear of falling at any moment, so too for mortals who are born, there is constant fear of death.
Just as all clay vessels made by a potter end in breakage,
so too is the life of mortals.
Both the young and the old, both the foolish and the wise—
All go under the power of death; all have death as their final destination.
For those who are overtaken by death as they depart for the next world, neither a father can save his son, nor can kinsmen save their kin.
Behold the various ways in which kinsmen lament for one who is being watched;
each and every mortal is led away like an ox to the slaughter.
Thus is the world struck down by death and by old age.
Therefore, the wise do not grieve, having understood the course of the world.
Look also at others as they go along, men following their karma;
having fallen under the power of Death, living beings here tremble.
In whatever way they conceive it,
it turns out otherwise than that;
such is its nature of separation.
"Behold how the world revolves"—
as it is said in the Suttas:
"Just as massive mountains..."
Reaching up to touch the sky,
they would burn, circling all around and crushing [everything] in the four directions.
Thus do old age and death overcome all living beings—
whether they be kshatriyas, brahmins, or vaishyas.
Even a Caṇḍāla or a Pakkusa,
he avoids nothing at all;
he tramples everything underfoot.
There, neither elephants nor ground, nor chariots nor infantry,
nor even by battle of spells or by wealth, can achieve victory.
Therefore, a wise person—
Clearly perceiving his own welfare,
the wise one should establish his confidence in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.
"One who lives by the Dhamma in body, speech, and mind—
him they praise in this very world, and he rejoices in the afterlife.
[As stated in the Pabbatū mama Sutta.]
Just as a full river carries away trees growing on its banks,
so too are all living beings swept away by old age and death.
For even the young die.
Whether man or woman,
what confidence can there be therein for a person,
when youth is but a fleeting life?
Some who were seen by many people at evening are not seen in the morning;
some who were seen by many people in the morning are not seen in the evening.
One must exert oneself this very day; for who knows if death will come tomorrow?
"There is no confusion for one by that Great Army, Death" (as stated in the Jātakas).
"There is no other here who instructs; speak to yourself alone."
Following the instructions of the Conqueror, the bhikkhu who fears cyclic existence [thinks]:
"Even a snake might bite me, or others who bear poison;
they might even kill me, and pains might arise within me."
The army of Death is beyond counting, with its calamities both external and internal;
by these, life is oppressed and cut short— one will die even today,
like marrow [consumed] by worms, cattle, thieves, or enemies.
Due to frequent disturbances, even from the ninety-six types of diseases,
and despite the many benefits provided by others, such as food, water, and the like,
I am constantly oppressed and shall die; may my life-span cease this very day.
The pitiless Death discharges many weapons at him who dwells in the battle of existence,
though he has no shelter; yet no one is released from those weapons—
not even those who are mighty in strength, great in wisdom, possessed of great psychic power, or great wealth.
Even though the Fully Enlightened One, the Lord of the entire world,
was my equal in age and seniority, he was slain by those very weapons;
likewise shall I too die, for I have made merit as my refuge.
The earth, water, fire, and air are the elements;
food, drink, and so forth are the nutriments;
cold, heat, and moisture are these [three].
The humors are bile, phlegm, and wind.
When these humors and the bodily elements and food are in equilibrium, the wind remains stable;
when they are in disequilibrium, even a small amount [of wind] is cut off at that very moment, being dependent on other factors.
The elements would destroy his humors, and he would be ill and unfit even for tomorrow;
what could an unfit person accomplish, even with effort at a time when he is fit?
Even tomorrow pains might arise—unpleasant, painful, and harsh.
Better to begin [right] now than to feel regret later.
For beings who have performed base deeds, even seeking refuge is terrifying;
I do not distinguish between the base and the noble, nor even when death is close at hand.
For beings oppressed by their own karma, fear arises even for a moment;
one might die this very day or tomorrow, so it is not right to be negligent.
When merit is exhausted, people perish quickly, even without any other cause.
I shall die with a pure mind, not with a defiled heart.
Although there are many existences remaining for me to undergo, let my life be cut short even now;
it is better to die a noble death than to live on.
When the destruction of beings through their own kamma is imminent,
the wise man stands firm, perceiving misfortune as having the form of fortune.
A wise and mindful person, when close to death, should reflect only upon that very [truth].
Thinking thus, being virtuous, I am unable to commit evil.
A disciple of the Buddha, when approaching death, should think only of this;
thinking thus, being virtuous, he is never at all haughty.
The wise person should certainly reflect on death beforehand;
they should perform the deeds that ought to be done, and thus they do not grieve.
Perceiving that death is near, being heedful and discerning—
Even at the time of death, he is neither deluded nor sorrowful.
Conscious even as he passes away from death, that bhikkhu cleanses his own defilements; having passed away stainless, he is certainly not one who goes to a state of woe.
When death is near, he who—
perceiving it to be far off or through negligence—
does what ought not to be done, [is lost].
Then he grieves excessively. When death is near, the heedless one perceives it as distant;
beset by evil states, he broods with a dejected mind.
When death is near, one who is corrupted by hatred and stubbornness rejoices in some things and grieves for others;
thus attached to them, he suffers exceedingly.
When death is near, he does not quickly seek medical treatment.
Having fallen into an offense committed intentionally, he then laments.
When death is near, he is associated with householders and novices, and not with those who are compliant;
at that time, his face is turned toward the world.
When death was near, that deceiver, a corrupter of families, having fallen into wrong livelihood, passed away like an ill omen.
He was sorrowful with those who grieve and joyful with those who rejoice; he suffered in suffering and delighted in pleasure.
Diligent in worldly affairs, though he beheld Gijjhakūṭa, he fell away.
Afflicted by the sickness of the defilements, they will die blameless;
yet, like one suffering from the gnawing of worms, how could such a restless person attain a happy rebirth?
They will die without having reflected; the two duties will not be fulfilled;
they will die with their studies unmastered, lacking insight, indolent, and fallen away from compassion.
They will die without having reflected, following the sway of the defilements.
He has transgressed against the Fully Awakened Ones; there is no one equal to him in cruelty.
Seeking wealth through unrighteousness, he will die without remorse;
not even a thought for merit arose in him, and his mind has gone to hell.
Thinking, "I shall enjoy it," one accumulates wealth through unrighteous means without reflecting;
whatever has been accumulated, that remains right here, and he who is greedy for it becomes a ghost in his own lineage.
When wealth returns to the house, friends and kinsmen remain at the cemetery.
Whether well done or ill done, karma follows one who goes along.
Whether thinking "I shall kill" without reflection, or engaging in this world for some purpose,
or regardless of the future life, one who goes toward the lower realms is like a straight path leading to the abyss.
Reflecting thus, one should apply oneself; through the Dhamma, one seeks wealth.
One who performs meritorious deeds rejoices even at death because of their good fortune.
Constantly guarding the five precepts and giving according to one's ability—
Dwelling at the Uposatha at the proper time, one will always go to a happy destination.
Quickly wash away the stain from your bowl; death will surely come.
Freeing yourself from wrong thoughts, perform the meditation that ought to be done.
Many nights have passed, wasting away my life;
how can I continue to dwell joined with dullness and negligence?
While they laugh, intoxicated by their own joy, I shall be hewn down by the bonds of death.
Today I have escaped from the womb; who could not be joyful at this?
I am now facing death, numbered among the weapons of the Lord of Death.
This is the time to be hurried; let him who would look on wait and see.
One should see the pure and the worthy; death will come;
time must be spent.
There is no room for laughter or joy among those beset by death, who must depart this very day or tomorrow.
For those who are surely destined to leave, what is the use of dwelling in negligence?
The present moment alone is manifest; today or tomorrow it may pass away.
The future is exceedingly long, a succession without end.
The present moment alone is manifest; by death, that [moment] will be left behind.
To exert great effort regarding that which must be abandoned is useless.
The future life is exceedingly long and, without provisions for the journey, it is very difficult to cross;
therefore, one who sees the long-term goal should apply great effort toward that end.
Let faith bind the provisions for the journey, for they are to be sought right here;
one who travels without provisions will not find them in another existence and will suffer from the threefold misery.
To cross over saṃsāra, bind yourselves with great rafts.
Having crossed the ocean of existence by means of meditation, generosity, and virtue,
he consumes the people who indulge in sensual pleasures,
awakening them to the right and wrong times.
"Kante kante" is a term for meat-eaters,
like one who repeatedly drinks [the blood] of a deer;
thus should one seek sensual pleasures through the search for sensual pleasures.
In the view that there is light and darkness,
one who wanders through the course of time will surely fulfill the Dhamma that is to be fulfilled.
Thinking, "I might die," one who is undismayed would not dare to do evil;
nor would he act with laughter, delight, frivolity, or negligence.
Thinking, "I might die," one who is stirred with urgency seeks only for a refuge.
Neither was there grief nor even joy, nor was there ever any restlessness.
Amidst the towering fires of disease, amidst terrifying and extreme exhaustion,
and as death drew near, it was like the gift of merit that bestows happiness.
Tearing themselves away from their circle of kinsmen, greatly distressed at the end of life,
even those who must depart leaving everything behind should rejoice if they are possessors of merit—
seeing the auspicious signs made manifest by their own karma.
At the time of death, rejoicing in the meritorious deeds one has performed—
those pleasant gifts of merit— one will easily attain a happy rebirth even amidst such great terror; therefore, these should be done beforehand.
When the divine messengers have made him confess his own deeds, if the being, when questioned by Yama,
remembers the merit he performed, he will go to a happy destination.
But even as he is dragged toward hell, his mind remains set on suffering.
Whatever merit liberates one from suffering, that indeed should always be performed.
For just as evil is to be abandoned, so too is merit to be relinquished;
having cast off both like a lamp dispelling darkness, one is like a bird that has shed its old skin.
Tearing themselves away from their circles of kinsmen, intensely distressed at the end of life,
sinners depart, leaving everything behind, terrified by the horrors [of hell].
They behold ill omens made manifest by their own karma.
Death is exceedingly painful, as are the deeds one has done while being urged on.
When there is such great terror, these evil oppressions lead swiftly to a miserable rebirth; therefore, one should indeed strive to avoid them.
Having confessed his negligence before the divine messengers and being questioned by King Yama,
he cried out against his own heedlessness as he fell swiftly into the great fire.
"I did no merit," he said, O Lord of Kings, when questioned by Yama.
Speaking thus of negligence, he quickly went to great suffering.
Having committed no evil, yet being questioned by the Lord of Death,
speaking thus of negligence, he quickly swallowed glowing sugar-candy.
The newborn, the aged, the sick, the dead, and the wise—these five are messengers of the gods;
seeing them, one should enter upon a state of spiritual urgency.
Those men who, though urged by the messengers of the gods, remain heedless;
Those who delight in lowly bodies will grieve for a long time,
being intent on the two burdens and fond of household chores and the like.
How can such a person remain on Gijjhakūṭa, that abode of the hungry ghosts?
One who studies the scriptures but does not practice them, being lazy and of poor resolve—
such a person [is lost].
What does that mountain remain for?
For those who have gone forth for the sake of liberation but are defiled and negligent, they have fallen even from a good rebirth; they are indeed very far from liberation.
Just as stones, whether large or small, sink when cast into water,
so too do people fall into a state of woe through even a minor evil deed.
Falling by means of that very minor act, they are further oppressed by many more.
Those who do not find an opportunity for liberation should not commit even a minor evil.
Having become loathsome due to their bloated bellies, they remain there constantly impure;
overwhelmed by suffering upon suffering, they are unable to rejoice or be glad.
Puñña of exceeding virtue,
Mahāyasa Sirindharo,
dwelt within the womb in the seed.
It is a matter of extreme shame:
the suffering of death occurs in an instant, but beyond that, it is even more painful;
the connection within the womb of a woman and the process of taking form there is truly terrifying.
The suffering of death is but momentary, while the suffering of long duration is extreme;
the transition between the raw and the cooked is a terrifying state of support.
Listen: that suffering exists even for one established in a high-born family.
In the womb, which is exceedingly cramped, like a loathsome water-skin,
filled with excrement, phlegm, and the like, and permeated by an extreme stench—
just as a worm in a cesspool might do so out of its own past karma— one was born there in darkness.
The body of atoms remains like a sufferer in hell;
constantly afflicted, mixed with pleasure, between the stomach and the intestines;
growing while being tormented by sensation, it is as if mindless and motionless.
Within ten months in the womb, many living beings die;
that which is fully matured is released from the exceedingly narrow birth canal.
With limbs covered in filth,
one gives birth with great exhaustion.
Thus, death, the transition, and the terrifying process of birth— these are what must be understood.
Seeing this and becoming disenchanted, the peaceful one may become free from passion for the double-bond of existence.
Thus, constantly recollect death and the stream [of rebirth];
even the best of kings, endowed with that mindfulness, would not desire the beginning of existence.
Without reflecting on the suffering in existence,
one repeatedly gives merit prompted by the hope for existence, rather than the excellent peace of Nibbāna.
Having discerned the suffering in existence, that which is prompted by disenchantment—
Having transcended existence through merit, Nibbāna bestows the peace of extinction.
Recalling the suffering in existence— the succession of death and birth and so forth—
one should become dispassionate toward the three realms of existence, just as a husband becomes weary of his own house.
A noble person performing meritorious deeds, mindful of the suffering at the transition [to death],
should, with a mind inclined toward disenchantment, avoid craving for existence.
Even in a place reborn through merit, there arises the occurrence of a transition into loathsomeness.
Therefore, O wise one, abandon that attachment, for existence is full of suffering. 3.
Exposition on the Meditation on the Foul:
Having seen a beautiful courtesan, in order to subdue one whose mind is lustful—
Having shown her the corpse of the dead man, the Conqueror said this to her:
“Whether walking or standing, sitting or lying down;
whether contracting or extending—the movement of the body is this very agitation.”
The body is bound together by sinews, plastered over with skin and flesh;
covered by the outer skin, it is not seen as it truly is.
It is filled with intestines, filled with entrails, with liver, heart, and kidneys.
Of the heart, of the lungs, of the kidneys, and of the spleen;
of mucus, of saliva, of sweat, and of fat;
of blood, of synovial fluid, of bile, and of grease.
Then from its nine streams, impurity flows out at all times:
eye-secretion from the eyes, ear-secretion from the ears,
mucus from the nose, and sometimes vomit from the mouth.
Bile and phlegm are vomited up, as are sweat and grime from the body.
Then his hollow head is filled with brain matter.
The fool, led by ignorance, considers it beautiful;
yet when he lies dead, [he realizes otherwise].
Swollen and discolored,
cast away in the charnel ground,
the relatives remain indifferent.
Dogs and jackals devour him, as do worms;
crows and vultures devour him, as do whatever other creatures there may be.
Having heard the word of the Buddha, a wise bhikkhu here—
One fully understands suffering, for one sees it as it truly is:
as this is, so is that; as that is, so is this. Both internally and externally, one should cause desire for the body to fade away.
Free from desire and passion, that wise bhikkhu here has attained the deathless peace,
Nibbāna, the state beyond death. He who, being two-footed,
is impure, foul-smelling, and repulsive— [such a one is surpassed by him].
Filled with various kinds of corpses, oozing here and there—
what else could it be but a lack of vision that one would think to exalt oneself or despise another because of such a body?
The *Kāyavicchandanīya-sutta* may also be called the *Vijaya-suttanta*.
The letter *ra* is like fire; it comes forth like fire itself.
Therefore, it should be called *rāga* (lust); craving indeed is what causes perpetual burning.
The fire of passion constantly burns those who perceive beauty;
like the pain of worms devouring [one's own] excrement, such a lustful person is always miserable.
Even when suffering, one seeks what is dear, and even having obtained it, one suffers because it is not complete.
There is no filling of the mass of the fire of passion by means of the fuel of the beloved;
there is no fire equal to passion—
thus it was said by the Great Seer.
Burnt by that fire of passion, the entire world suffers from the three kinds of suffering.
By one person, milk was drunk; by four, curd; and water was abundant.
The cause of passion is the link in existence, a station without end or beginning.
More than four hundred times, there has been the blood from the severing of my head;
the cause of passion, O mortal, is the fear that is without end or beginning.
The tears shed by one person who weeps are more abundant than four oceans of milk;
because of that, there is lamentation, and suffering that is without discoverable beginning.
[There is also] the swallowing of glowing coals, being burned by the fire of execution, and so forth.
Because of that, he experienced immeasurable great suffering in hell.
Even during the arising of one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas, he was not liberated;
because of that, he experienced the parching torment of hunger and thirst as a hungry ghost.
In the animal realm and among the asuras, one experiences manifold suffering;
throughout this beginningless saṃsāra, all of it is rooted in passion.
For a single individual, over the course of a single eon, the accumulation [of bones] would reach sixty cartloads.
If it were gathered together, it would exceed Mount Vepulla.
This suffering lasts for one eon; what need is there to speak of many eons?
Is not lust a great enemy? Yet foolish people long for it.
Purity from passion, freedom from sorrow, being free from suffering, having attained the right method,
and the direct realization of Nibbāna— these are considered the five fruits of the meditation on the foul (asubha).
For the meditator who grasps the foul, there is moderation and restraint of the sense faculties.
These six are the supreme words uttered by the Soma-possessing Sage for the purification of lust:
for those who are constantly afflicted by the disease of passion, foulness (*asubha*) is a potent medicinal herb;
for those seized by the yakṣa of lust, foulness is the unsurpassed mantra.
The impurities are considered to be of two kinds: with life and without life.
Those with life consist of hair, body hair, and so forth; these ten are those without life.
The bloated, the livid, the festering, and the fissured;
The devoured, the scattered, the hacked and scattered, the bleeding, the worm-infested,
and the skeleton— having obtained any one of these while mindful,
he would see them as clearly in his mind as a treasure in the forest.
The bloated, the being eaten, and that with flesh, the bloodless and fleshless;
the scattered, the bleached white heap of bones—thus, in nine ways, one contemplates the foulness of corpses.
Freed from death, I turn back from this cemetery.
Having understood the purpose, one who feels revulsion should rejoice.
For the sake of revulsion toward what is living, that which is lifeless is declared beautiful:
"This body is like that; it will surely become just so."
Such is the nature of this body, such its destiny, it cannot transcend this;
having observed this, one should reflect upon those who have died one or two days ago, and so forth: as this is, so was that; as that was, so is this.
One should direct one's attention to the loathsomeness and repulsiveness of the body:
its bloated state, its livid color,
and so forth— repulsive and disgusting.
In the same way, this body of mine is also thus;
there is no difference except for the duration of life.
Whether bloated or livid, there is nothing beautiful about it whatsoever.
Even when searching thoroughly within this body of mine,
one would find only the elements of repulsiveness and the two kinds of fat.
Desiring dispassion toward oneself, one should contemplate this body in this way.
By color, shape, and smell, by its location and its coughing,
and because it is disgusting and repulsive, the hair of the head is not to be delighted in.
Thus one should contemplate the hair of the head.
This same method applies to the body hairs and so forth;
for one should review each of the thirty-two parts individually.
That which has emerged from the body is loathsome and disgusting;
even that which has not yet emerged is as loathsome and disgusting as it is.
Just as feces, even when processed, never attains a state of pleasantness.
Even with thousands of efforts, the hair and so forth remain thus;
their intrinsic nature is indeed repulsive, like even a single heap of excrement.
Is there not even greater loathsomeness in thirty-two heaps of excrement?
Even individually, things such as hair are repulsive by their very nature;
how much more so, then, is this heap consisting of the thirty-two parts beginning with hair?
When these very same attractive parts are gathered together into a single mass, that mass itself becomes attractive.
Among those things that are gathered together, though they are undesirable, that collection itself is undesirable.
When they are separated from one another— as in the case of hair, body hair, nails, and so forth—
that [collection] no longer exists, just as a young girl does not exist apart from her face, hands, and other [limbs].
They are merely lumped together among those very things;
from where could those various things have come?
This is nothing more than a mere designation.
There is no such thing as disgust for the unwholesome.

One should contemplate what is wholesome, not what is unwholesome; for one who contemplates the wholesome there is happiness, while one who imagines the unwholesome is tormented by manifold sufferings.
One who perceives beauty should not fail to cultivate the perception of the non-blameworthy, the peaceful, and the repulsive.
To one who perceives beauty, the fire of lust arises with the thought, "The woman is beautiful.
One should see her as non-existent and unreal through the blazing fire of passion.
By that [ignorance], one never perceives what is peaceful and real:
the milk drunk by one person, the blood from the severed head of another,
and the tears shed for that reason— these together are more water than the four oceans.
Even in the future, as he wanders through saṃsāra, there will be just as much;
if one would slay passion without effort, even milk would become blood and tears.
He has grown through the perception of beauty.
In its absence, that [mind] perishes;
it cannot be firmly struck by one whose energy is lax,
for that is not the perception of such a person.
Having aroused intense energy, one should cultivate the meditation on the foul for the sake of abandoning the perception of beauty, even at the cost of one's life.
Remaining indifferent toward other duties, one should cultivate the meditation on the foul.
Having become one whose fire of passion is now feeble here, it will be extinguished in the future.
Thinking, "This is my only task," one should cultivate the meditation on the foul;
having thus become one with a feeble fire, one will indeed attain gladness.
Failing to see the loathsomeness that is to be seen in the body,
the heedless man, finding no cause for joy, does not even delight in the going-forth.
"Before I die, while I am still in this body, let me see what is worth seeing."
Having obtained freedom from desire, he rejoices exceedingly in the going-forth.
Failing to see the loathsomeness to be seen in the body, through negligence,
he has gone to the state of a great outcaste, having in vain passed beyond that which is so difficult to attain.
One who desires to see what is present and real within this body—
namely, that which is loathsome and unseen due to the fire of passion—
should examine it repeatedly with the light of the lamp of wisdom, remaining ever mindful.
With the lamp of wisdom, one who is skilled should not be a lustful seeker.
With this body that is loathsome and has been cast out by the loathing [of the wise],

If you fear suffering, and if suffering is not dear to you;
Commit no evil deed, whether openly or in secret.

Extinguish the fire of passion with equanimity toward what has burned your head.
Quickly, by means of the perception of foulness,

Based upon their virtues, the conceit "I am" arises in those possessed of virtue.
By reflecting on death, cast down the banner of pride.

He should contemplate the body as foul, for such a vision is beneficial at all times.
One would waste time in vain, even if one were to become ill.
Seeing the body with revulsion and reflecting upon its childish nature,

He should neither look upon nor think of the various limbs of women.

Faith is stirred by the mind, and it is lofty and performs lofty deeds.
Craving delights in what is beautiful to see; faith has good conduct and devotion as its food.
Craving wanders in a scattered way; faith moves with clarity.
Craving defiles the mind and, together with its attendants, brings endless suffering;
faith clarifies the mind and, following along with the self, brings happiness.
Thus, know truly the distinction between craving and faith.
Having understood this, one should destroy craving and cultivate faith in the heart.
For even sugar-cane crushed in a machine, or sandalwood ground to powder,
remains sweet and fragrant— even when harmed, a person remains like loving-kindness.
Just as sandalwood is perfumed by its fragrance,
so too does the virtuous person perfume even themselves with the sweet scent of loving-kindness.
Sandalwood powder, even when dry, never becomes foul-smelling.
In the same way, even when fallen into suffering, a virtuous person does not commit evil.
One should forgive a fault for the sake of the goal, remembering the patience of the Buddha;
even toward an enemy, one who is soaked in loving-kindness should harbor no resentment.
Abuse does not reach me; it is only the one who reviles me who suffers.
Knowing this, the wise person should not revile anyone at all.
"May abuse not come to me."
He is the one who causes that very thing to perish; knowing this,
one should endure and not utter abuse in return.
The abuser took his way,
but the counter-shout was not the better course; the Buddha would not have followed after him.
May he not become even worse than that.
Craving and ignorance are the two roots of the poisonous tree of saṃsāra;
of all the teachings of the True Dharma, only these two bear sweet fruit.
Purify the mind through effort; that which is purified by effort brings happiness beyond measure.
Unpurified, it is defiled and brings suffering. Purified, it leads to a happy destination;
unpurified, it leads to an unhappy destination.
Purify the mind; do not stain it with the impurities of lust and hatred.
He by whom the stains born of aversion have been destroyed is one who truly dwells in the Teaching.
Having understood that there is no other purpose in grasping it,
may the Buddha destroy that duality.
Having built his dwelling in Raṇakuṇava, he went to see [his parents] in the east.
Thus it was composed by the Elder Vāsava, who possesses the foremost qualities.
